t.5.34.1: Once more the greatly radiant Hanūmān, son of the Wind, spoke courteous words in order to win Sītā's trust.
t.5.34.2: I am a monkey, O most fortunate lady, the messenger of the wise Rāma; and behold, O queen, this ring marked with Rāma's name. Take heart, may good fortune be yours, for the fruit of your sorrow is now spent.
t.5.34.3: Taking her husband's hand-ornament and gazing at it, Jānakī became joyful, as though she had been reunited with her husband himself.
t.5.34.4: That lovely face of hers, with its long eyes of copper and white, became radiant with delight, like the king of the stars, the moon, released from Rāhu.
t.5.34.5: Then that modest young woman, delighted by her husband's message and well pleased at hearing the welcome news, praised the great monkey.
t.5.34.6: You are valiant, you are capable, you are wise, O best of monkeys, for by you alone this realm of the rākṣasas has been overpowered.
t.5.34.7: The ocean, abode of sea-monsters, spreading a hundred yojanas wide, was made like a cow's hoofprint by the one striding across it, praiseworthy for his valor.
t.5.34.8: Indeed, I do not consider you an ordinary monkey, O bull among monkeys, you who have no terror of Rāvaṇa, nor even any agitation.
t.5.34.9: And, O best of monkeys, you are worthy of being spoken to by me, if indeed you have been sent by that Rāma, whose self is known.
t.5.34.10: For the invincible Rāma would surely not send an untested messenger without knowing his prowess, least of all into my presence.
t.5.34.11: By good fortune the righteous-souled Rāma, devoted to dharma, is well, and so too is the greatly splendid Lakṣmaṇa, who increases the joy of Sumitrā.
t.5.34.12: If Kākutstha is well, why then does he not, risen up like the fire at the end of an age, burn in his wrath this earth girdled by the ocean?
t.5.34.13: Or rather, those two are capable of subduing even the gods; but for me alone, I think, there is no reversal of my sorrows.
t.5.34.14: Is Rāma troubled at all? I hope he is not consumed by anguish. And is that best of men carrying out the tasks that lie ahead?
t.5.34.15: I hope the king's son is not dejected or agitated, and that he is not bewildered in the tasks before him? I hope he is performing deeds worthy of a man?
t.5.34.16: Does that scorcher of foes, eager for victory and a true friend, employ the twofold means and also the threefold means in dealing with his friends?
t.5.34.17: Does he win friends, and is he sought out by his friends? Does he have noble friends, and is he held in honour by his friends?
t.5.34.18: Does the son of the king hope for the grace of the gods? Does he rely upon both human effort and destiny?
t.5.34.20: Rāma has always been accustomed to comforts and unaccustomed to hardships. Now that he has met with this supreme sorrow, I hope he does not sink into despair?
t.5.34.19: I hope Rāghava has not lost his affection for me because of our separation? Will the monkey free me from this misfortune?
t.5.34.21: And likewise, I hope news of the welfare of Kausalyā, and of Sumitrā too, is heard often? And is the welfare of Bharata heard of as well?
t.5.34.22: Is Rāghava, who is worthy of honour, stricken with grief on my account? Surely Rāma's mind is not set on another? Will he rescue me?
t.5.34.23: Will Bharata, so devoted to his brother, send for my sake a fearsome akṣauhiṇī, a bannered army guarded by his ministers?
t.5.34.24: Will the glorious Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, come for my sake, surrounded by heroic monkeys whose weapons are their teeth and claws?
t.5.34.25: And will the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, who increases the joy of Sumitrā and is skilled in weapons, scatter the rākṣasas with a net of arrows?
t.5.34.26: Shall I, I wonder, soon see Rāvaṇa, together with his kinsmen and allies, slain in battle by Rāma with a fierce missile?
t.5.34.27: I hope that face of his, golden in hue and fragrant as a lotus, is not withering without me, wretched with grief, like a lotus scorched by the sun when the water has dried away?
t.5.34.28: He who felt no distress, no fear and no grief when, at the bidding of dharma, he gave up the kingdom and led me on foot into the forest, does he still keep some steadfastness in his heart?
t.5.34.30: Having thus spoken to that lord of monkeys words of great import and sweet meaning, the queen, the lovely lady, fell silent, wishing to hear again his delightful speech concerning Rāma.
t.5.34.29: Neither his mother nor his father nor anyone else surpasses me in affection for him, or is even my equal. O messenger, this will to live of mine lasts only so long as I may hear news of my beloved.
t.5.34.31: Having heard the words of Sītā, Māruti of formidable prowess placed his joined palms upon his head and spoke words in reply.
t.5.34.32: Lotus-eyed Rāma does not know that you are here. But as soon as he hears my words, Rāghava will come swiftly.
t.5.34.33: Leading forth a mighty army thronged with hosts of monkeys and bears, and checking with floods of arrows the unshakable abode of Varuṇa, Kākutstha will make the city of Laṅkā one whose rākṣasas are stilled.
t.5.34.34: There, should Death himself, or should the gods together with the asuras, stand in the way of Rāma, he will slay even them.
t.5.34.35: O noble lady, overwhelmed by the grief born of not seeing you, Rāma finds no peace, like an elephant tormented by a lion.
t.5.34.36: O Devī, I swear to you by Dardara and by the roots and fruits, by Malaya and Vindhya, by Meru and by Mandara.
t.5.34.38: Soon, O Vaidehī, you will see Rāma on Mount Prasravaṇa, seated like Śatakratu upon the summit of the vault of heaven.
t.5.34.37: So shall you behold the face of Rāma, lovely, with beautiful eyes, lips like the bimba fruit and handsome earrings, like the full moon that has risen.
t.5.34.40: With his inmost self wholly absorbed in you, Rāghava does not brush from his body the gadflies, nor the mosquitoes, nor the insects, nor the creeping things.
t.5.34.39: Rāghava does not eat meat, nor does he take honey. He always eats only the fifth meal, of wild forest fare, properly prepared.
t.5.34.41: Rāma is ever absorbed in meditation, ever given over to grief; he thinks of nothing else at all, for he has fallen under the sway of love.
t.5.34.42: Rāma, the best of men, is ever sleepless; and even when he has fallen asleep, he wakes up uttering the sweet word "Sītā."
t.5.34.43: Seeing a fruit or a flower, or whatever else delights the heart of a woman, he sighs again and again and calls out to you, 'Alas, my beloved!'
t.5.34.44: O queen, that great-souled prince, ever tormented with grief and calling out to you alone, saying "Sītā!", holds firm to his vow and has made every effort for the sole purpose of winning you back.
t.5.34.45: Her sorrow dispelled by the praise of Rāma, yet grieving with a grief equal to Rāma's grief, the daughter of the Videha king became like a night at the onset of autumn, whose moon is still veiled by lingering clouds.
